the set theoretic type system variant has one issue I think the algebraic one avoids: An overlap between types is ambiguous, i.e. "int | int" doesn't make any sense to write. In a function parse_postal_code, where you either get the postal code, or an error code you wouldn't be able to differentiate. You could write your own types for that, but now you've essentially recreated what the algebraic versions do by forcing a selection through the type constructor on the inner type instead of the wrapping union type.

That being said, in cases where there is no overlap I don't see why "the old way" shouldn't behave like typescript through implicit conversion as there is only one applicable constructor. Forcing explicit selection if there is overlap, but do it automatically when there is none seems like reasonable behavior that is a strict superset of what you wrote before.

No, it's not just the format description, even though the format description incorporates useless fields that are designed specifically to help setuptools to overcome the problems they created for themselves (all the "Dynamic" stuff is worthless otherwise).

Packaging, in this context, means a unified interface that describes to the tool what needs to happen to the source code in order for it to be transformed into a binary package. There are about a dozen tools that can package Python binary modules, setuptools, SWIG, bind11 and so on. Each does it in a completely different way. In practice, if you want to build the packages now available on PyPI, you will not be able to come up with a single tool that can build every one of them, probably, not even half of them.

All this talk about standardized metadata is worthless because of what actually goes into the package. The metadata is the least of your problems when packaging Python code.

Copyright in compilation would be sufficient alone, requiring no new laws, to my reading. In particular:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_in_compilation

> In the copyright law in the United States, such copyright may exist when the materials in the compilation (or "collective work") are selected, coordinated, or arranged creatively such that a new work is produced. Copyright does not exist when content is compiled without creativity, such as in the production of a telephone directory. In the case of compilation copyright, the compiler does not receive copyright in the underlying material, but only in the selection, coordination, or arrangement of that material.

All my experience seeing orgs ship real production code with the assistance of AI over months/many-thousands-of-commits shows that the skill not only lies in what context you choose to provide in the first place (product and technical specifications, design guidelines, prompting process with the model(s)), but also in how to effectively review and test all of it, which is still done with human direction throughout. This is why people with no experience in coding can't do with AI what an industry veteran with 20 years shipping to production can.

In any case, I think existing reading of copyright law will be sufficient to say that large AI-driven software projects are a process of orchestration and also of curation in selecting what actually gets committed (or, if commit-by-default is enabled, then what to revert). This may not always be true in the future, though, as capabilities increase...one part of me thinks you could just do random stuff like "Make me an excel except every cell is a powerpoint presentation" and a good enough AI would reason through and produce something without further input. But I think in most cases, folks have a real set of requirements in mind, and get all of them into the AI through a process of iteration in various ways. I think that's real work that requires skill and, in many cases, creativity, at least in the sense that someone else walking up to the same tool and prompting on their own would produce a very different output than you'd see if you asked the same person to retry the same project.

Time will tell.
